podcasts.title: The brain helped us build AI. Now AI is explaining the brain.
podcasts.description:
The human brain remains one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in science. We have roughly 86 billion neurons firing in a way that somehow produces intelligence, and yet the brain is still largely a black box. In the early days of AI, researchers looked to the brain for clues about how to build smarter machines. But today, that relationship has been flipped on its head. Join Professor Hannah Fry and neuroscience researchers Maria Eckstein and Kim Stachenfeld to see how scientists are using AI to better understand the human mind. podcasts.title: How To Build A Jet Engine From Scratch
podcasts.description:
On November 21, 2026, Boom Supersonic (YC W16) fired their prototype engine core for the first time.


They're developing a shared core for two products: Superpower, a natural-gas turbine for AI data centers, and Symphony, the engine intended for the Overture supersonic airliner. The turbine business could help fund Overture while giving Symphony years of real-world operating data before it ever flies.


In this episode of Hard Tech, Boom founder and CEO Blake Scholl shows YC's Jared Friedman around their new Superpower Superfactory in Colorado and explains how they’re building a jet engine from scratch.


On the factory floor, we explore in-house manufacturing, the challenge of making turbine blades survive extreme heat, and the custom software Boom uses to design and iterate on engine parts.

podcasts.title: OpenAI’s Noam Brown: Why Game Theory Didn’t Lead to General Intelligence (Live at No Limit Finals)
podcasts.description:
Noam Brown built the first AIs to beat top poker professionals, then concluded that game theory, the field his career was built on, was not the path to general intelligence. Recorded live at the Finals of No Limit, Sequoia’s pokerbot tournament, the OpenAI researcher describes his “crisis of faith”: game theory assumes everyone is rational, and the Diplomacy bots that won were the ones trained on human data to model how people actually behave in the messy real world. That sent him to OpenAI and the work that became o1, at a time when much of the field believed a bigger pre-trained model would solve everything. Noam explains why he asks every new model to build a pokerbot, where GPT-6 Astra still falls short, and why this is the “centaur period” of human plus AI. He argues that human progress has always been one giant recursive self-improvement loop, and shares his most controversial take: promising students should drop out and join the labs now.



Hosted by Alfred Lin, Sequoia CapitalChapters:

0:00 – Introduction

0:09 – Why poker: a perfect strategy nobody knew

2:12 – How Noam would build a pokerbot in 60 minutes

4:37 – From poker to Diplomacy: where game theory breaks on irrational humans

9:39 – A crisis of faith and the bet on reasoning over bigger pre-training

13:01 – The unlock: models that think before acting

14:59 – The centaur period, and what gamers and AI researchers share

18:13 – Audience Q&A: why models still can't build a great pokerbot alone

22:02 – Is chain of thought the right way to scale test-time compute?

23:42 – RSI and the case for dropping out to join the labs

27:54 – Lightning round: unsolved games and AI at the World Series of Poker

podcasts.title: E259｜机械神教与反人性策略：华尔街量化巨头的AI之路
podcasts.description:
华尔街最低调、最赚钱的那一批量化交易巨头，也是这一轮AI浪潮里囤算力、抢人才、投资AI实验室最凶猛的那一批。
他们不靠市场趋势赚钱，而是靠波动和速度在毫秒间争夺价差。和大家印象中西装革履的金融人士并不一样，这些公司里的人可能是一群数学家、物理学家，他们把市场当成一个纯粹的客观的自然现象来研究，寻找其中的规律。他们信奉“肉身苦弱，机械飞升”，不愿让个人主观判断干预模型。也正因如此，算力成了他们最重要的运营开支之一。
本期硅谷101播客，我们邀请到两位来自量化巨头XTX Markets、DRW内部的研究者，揭秘AI量化的底层逻辑，探究这个行业能不能被AI改变、会怎么样被AI改变。
我们聊到了很多有意思的观点，比如说，通用大模型的突飞猛进，并没有从根本上改变量化模型。因为市场是一个高维、连续、难以完全定义的不可观察系统，比自然语言要复杂得多。嘉宾们认为，量化模型可能更接近是FSD或机器人模型。量化模型和AI前沿实验室的进化策略也完全不同，AI Lab会把所有的算力和人才集中押注在一起，让模型一代比一代更聪明；但量化模型的策略是分散化的，需要永远尝试新的东西，做出完全不一样的模型，相互补充，形成组合。
而最大的不同，可能是金融行业对风险和纪律的敬畏。保证活下去，活得足够长，这是一个比赚钱更重要的问题。最终我们发现，表面上，量化交易公司几乎都变成了大大小小的AI实验室，华尔街和硅谷在抢同一批人才、同一批芯片，界限似乎正在消失。但不同的底层逻辑，仍然塑造了两个行业截然不同的风格与气质。

podcasts.title: Jensen Huang in 2009: The Charlie Rose Interview Before AI Changed the World
podcasts.description:
Jensen Huang was one of the most important business leaders in the world. He was co-founder and CEO of NVIDIA, the maker of chips critical to artificial intelligence.
As artificial intelligence became the focus of conversations about the future, he became famous around the world. He dramatically lost that position when it was disclosed he had a personal relationship with a woman suspected by officials in the intelligence community to be an asset of Chinese intelligence.
Before artificial intelligence became the story, I interviewed Jensen Huang in 2009.
We talked of many things, including NVIDIA, graphics processing technology, and the future of computing.

podcasts.title: ServiceNow’s Amit Zavery on How AI Agents Change the Software Business
podcasts.description:
ServiceNow’s Amit Zavery joins Motley Fool analyst Rachel Warren to explain why he thinks AI agents will change how enterprises buy and use software. He discusses the move from standalone AI pilots to agents built into everyday workflows, as well as the shift from seat licenses toward pricing tied to usage. They also cover what companies need to monitor and control as agents take on more work.

Topics covered:
• Why ServiceNow is moving beyond standalone, or “sidecar,” AI tools
• Lessons from scaling Google Cloud and working with customers’ existing systems
• How agents assist with IT incidents, employee onboarding, and customer service
• Seat licenses, usage pricing, and why enterprises still value predictable spending
• What separates AI pilots from deployments that deliver measurable results
• AI Control Tower, agent permissions, and runtime oversight
• ServiceNow Flow and how employees could get support inside tools like Slack and Teams

Interviewee: Amit Zavery, president, chief product officer, and chief operating officer of ServiceNow, as introduced in the interview.
Interviewer: Rachel Warren, Motley Fool analyst.

podcasts.title: Gavin Baker: Why Nvidia Needs Jensen Huang Back as CEO
podcasts.description:
Gavin Baker, Managing Partner & CIO of Atreides Management, joins Sourcery at TomorrowX to discuss Nvidia's leadership crisis, Jensen Huang's potential return, the AI market selloff, SpaceX's Starship breakthrough, and the future of orbital compute.

After 27 years investing in semiconductors and knowing Jensen Huang since 2000, Gavin explains why he and Brad Gerstner wrote a letter urging Nvidia's board to take a measured approach to its CEO decision. He makes the case for Jensen's leadership, warns about the consequences for American AI competitiveness, and explains why Nvidia's relationships with Taiwan's semiconductor supply chain may be nearly impossible to replicate.

On AI markets, Gavin argues that Wall Street is underestimating the scale of AI demand by focusing too heavily on frontier model revenue while overlooking enterprise AI infrastructure and the open-source ecosystem. He points to Michael Dell's AI factory sales, Fireworks AI's growth, and continued demand across the semiconductor industry.

Gavin also discusses SpaceX's latest Starship milestone, the economics of rapid rocket reusability, the potential for orbital data centers, Starlink direct-to-cell connectivity, and his estimate that SpaceX's first-party AI business could be approaching $10 billion.

Topics covered:
- Nvidia's leadership crisis and Jensen Huang's potential comeback
- Gavin Baker and Brad Gerstner's letter to Nvidia's board
- Why AI infrastructure demand may be stronger than stock prices suggest
- The overlooked economics of open-source AI
- Nvidia, Huawei, Taiwan Semiconductor, and American AI competitiveness
- SpaceX's Starship breakthrough and orbital compute
- The future of Starlink and SpaceX's AI business

Recorded live at TomorrowX.
